scenes.title: The PostgreSQL 17 Query Planner

screen.heading: The PostgreSQL 17 Query Planner
lines: A comprehensive tutorial

narration.text: How does the PostgreSQL 17 query planner work? Let’s follow the tutorial from its main idea to its diagnosis steps.

scenes.title: What does the planner decide?

screen.heading: What does the planner decide?
lines: How does PostgreSQL 17 turn SQL into a plan?

narration.text: This tutorial asks how the PostgreSQL 17 query planner works, including its core mechanisms and extension interfaces. We will follow a query through planning and connect each subsystem to the decisions it changes.

scenes.title: A search over equivalent plans

screen.heading: The planner builds and compares candidates
lines: Useful alternatives survive the comparison

narration.text: The planner turns an analyzed and rewritten query into one executable plan. It first makes a working model and applies safe transformations. Then it builds candidates from the bottom up: ways to scan tables, join inputs, group, sort, and limit. Each candidate carries estimated rows and costs.

Candidates compete as they are built. The comparison also accounts for ordering, parameterization, and parallel safety. The cheapest final path becomes a plan tree. The planner entry point uses an installed planner hook, or the standard planner, and returns its output as a PlannedStmt.

scenes.title: From SQL text to execution

screen.heading: From SQL text to execution
lines: Raw parsing
Parse analysis and rewriting
Planning
Portal and executor

narration.text: Raw parsing checks syntax without consulting catalogs. Parse analysis uses catalog information and a snapshot to turn the statement into a typed Query. Rewriting expands views and applies rules, and can produce a list of queries. Planning then creates the executable statement that the portal and executor will run.

Utility statements require a distinction. They commonly carry a utility wrapper rather than an ordinary query plan. Utilities such as EXPLAIN and CREATE TABLE AS arrange planning of their inner query when the utility runs.

scenes.title: A Path is a candidate

screen.heading: A Path is a candidate
lines: RelOptInfo: a relation being planned
Path: one candidate way to produce its rows
Plan: executable tree
Useful properties can preserve alternatives

narration.text: A Path is one candidate way to produce a relation’s rows. A RelOptInfo groups alternatives for a base relation, a join relation, or an upper result. These are the planner’s working objects. The executable Plan tree is built later, from the chosen path.
Two candidates compete within the same relation. A path with a useful ordering or parameterization can survive alongside another with a lower total cost. Startup cost and parallel safety also matter.

scenes.title: The tutorial’s running database

screen.heading: Q1: the running query

code.content:
-- Q1: pending orders of western customers, largest first
SELECT /* wiki_pqt_q1 */ c.name, o.id, o.amount
  FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
 WHERE c.region = 'west' AND o.status = 'pending'
 ORDER BY o.amount DESC
 LIMIT 5;

narration.text: The examples use the page’s shop database: two thousand customers, thirty thousand orders, and ninety thousand item rows. The data is deliberately skewed. Thirty percent of orders belong to twenty large customers. The first query joins western customers to pending orders, orders by amount descending, and keeps five rows.

Keep the kinds of evidence distinct. EXPLAIN supplies planner estimates. Actual counts and catalog values are measurements. Arithmetic from quoted inputs is derived. The fixture uses statistics targets large enough to sample all its rows; larger tables at ordinary targets use random samples.

scenes.title: Q1: estimates beside observations

screen.heading: Q1: estimates beside observations
lines: Pending orders: estimated 3,019; actual 3,019
Western customers: estimated 200; actual 200
Join: estimated 302; actual 290
Hash Join → Sort → Limit

narration.text: Q1’s chosen plan scans orders and customers, builds a hash table, joins, sorts, and limits. The pending orders estimate is three thousand and nineteen, matching the run. Western customers are estimated at two hundred, also matching the run. The join estimate is three hundred and two; the observed count is two hundred and ninety.

The cost pair on a node is its estimated startup cost and total cost. Actual figures come from execution. Here the executor reports a top-N heapsort using twenty-five kilobytes; those runtime details are observations.

scenes.title: Simplify when the conditions allow it

screen.heading: Simplify when the conditions allow it
lines: Immutable constant expressions can fold
Simple subqueries can be pulled up
LIMIT / OFFSET and barriers can block changes
OFFSET 0 blocks pull-up and qual pushdown

narration.text: Before searching paths, preprocessing exposes an equivalent query that is easier to optimize. Immutable functions with constant arguments can be folded. Stable functions are treated differently: they may be folded for estimation without replacing the executable expression. Volatility and side effects constrain what is safe.

A simple subquery or view can be pulled into the parent’s join search. Aggregates, sorting, distinctness, limits, security barriers, and volatile outputs can block that change. In the page’s OFFSET zero example, both pull-up and filter pushdown are blocked.

scenes.title: Meaning and security constrain transformations

screen.heading: Meaning and security constrain transformations
lines: Strict WHERE conditions can reduce an outer join
The same condition in ON can preserve outer rows
Security level constrains condition order
Equivalence classes can derive restrictions

narration.text: A strict upper WHERE condition that rejects nulls on the nullable side can turn an outer join into an inner join. The same condition inside ON can preserve unmatched outer rows. Moving the condition changes meaning, so the planner’s transformation must respect its position and null behavior.

Security also constrains evaluation. Leaky user conditions must respect security levels; a sufficiently cheap leakproof condition may run earlier. Equalities provide another transformation: an equivalence class records expressions known to be equal.

scenes.title: Estimate size before estimating filters

screen.heading: Estimate size before estimating filters
lines: Stored rows per page × current pages
ANALYZE stores summaries
File growth can change total-row estimates
Width estimates also affect costs

narration.text: The planner normally estimates a table’s total rows from stored rows per page multiplied by the current file’s page count. This combines stored catalog information with a live size measurement. It does not count every row while planning. A growing file can therefore change the total estimate before a new ANALYZE.
ANALYZE stores summaries including common values, histogram bounds, null fractions, distinct counts, and correlation. It normally samples rows, so summaries can vary between runs.

scenes.title: Estimate the fraction that survives

screen.heading: Estimate the fraction that survives
lines: Selectivity: estimated fraction passing a condition
Equality can use common-value frequencies
Ranges use histograms and common values
Remaining conditions often multiply

narration.text: Selectivity is the estimated fraction of rows that pass a condition. Equality with a value in the most-common-values list can use that value’s stored frequency. Range estimates combine the common values with interpolation through histogram bounds. A missing statistic requires the relevant estimator’s fallback.
Q1’s pending frequency, applied to thirty thousand orders, gives three thousand and nineteen estimated rows. Conditions without applicable extended statistics often combine as independent fractions.

scenes.title: When columns are related

screen.heading: When columns are related
lines: region = west: frequency 0.1
country = PT: frequency 0.049
Independent estimate: 10 rows
Measured: 98 rows
Extended statistics and ANALYZE: estimate 98

narration.text: The page’s western Portuguese customers show the cost of independence. Multiplying two thousand by the western frequency, zero point one, and the Portuguese frequency, zero point zero four nine, gives nine point eight, displayed as ten rows. The measured result is ninety-eight because country determines region in this fixture.

The example creates extended statistics over region and country, then runs ANALYZE. The scan estimate rises to ninety-eight. Extended statistics describe columns or expressions of one table together. Creating the object alone does not populate its statistics.

scenes.title: File size and histograms can disagree

screen.heading: File size and histograms can disagree
lines: Live page count can grow
Stored histogram bounds can stay stale
A B-tree endpoint probe can refine an estimate
The page’s range example: 2 estimated; 10,000 actual

narration.text: A file can grow while its histogram remains unchanged. In the page’s isolated range example, the table receives more rows after ANALYZE. The total-row estimate scales with the file, but the histogram still ends at ten thousand. A condition beyond that endpoint estimates two rows and actually returns ten thousand.

A suitable plain, non-partial B-tree with the compared column first permits a probe of the live endpoint. In this example it raises the estimate to one hundred and ninety-eight, still far below the observed result. ANALYZE refreshes the summaries. Live file size alone does not refresh a histogram.

scenes.title: Cost is an estimate in planner units

screen.heading: Cost is an estimate in planner units
lines: Startup: work before the first row
Total: work for all rows
Default seq_page_cost: 1.0
Default random_page_cost: 4.0
effective_cache_size models available cache

narration.text: Cost is the planner’s estimate of how expensive a step is. Startup cost represents work before the first row can be returned; total cost represents all rows. These are planner units rather than milliseconds. The model combines page access, tuple processing, operators, and other work using configured prices.
The default sequential page price is one, and the random page price is four. The effective cache size setting helps model how many pages might stay cached; it reserves no memory.

scenes.title: A sequential scan’s price

screen.heading: A sequential scan’s price
lines: orders: 226 pages and 30,000 rows
Plain scan cost: 526
One pending-status condition: 601
Filter cost is charged across scanned rows

narration.text: The page derives an orders scan directly. There are two hundred and twenty-six pages and thirty thousand rows. With a sequential page price of one and tuple processing at zero point zero one, the plain scan totals five hundred and twenty-six planner cost units.

Adding the pending-status comparison adds the default operator price for every scanned row. That gives six hundred and one. The costing model also does not credit short-circuit evaluation as if every later condition were automatically skipped.

scenes.title: An eligible index can still lose on cost

screen.heading: An eligible index can still lose on cost
lines: Bitmap plan: 513.47
Forced alternative index plan: 1,140.74
Lower random-page price: index cost 453.57
The example changes costs, not index eligibility

narration.text: For the page’s customer identifier range, the bitmap plan costs five hundred and thirteen point four seven. Forced settings expose an eligible index scan at one thousand one hundred and forty point seven four. Its existence shows that the ordinary bitmap choice is a cost comparison, not failure to recognize the index.

In another forced leg, lowering random page cost to one point one brings the index alternative to four hundred and fifty-three point five seven. These fixture probes reveal alternatives; they are not recommendations for a server’s settings.

scenes.title: Memory changes modeled and observed work

screen.heading: Memory changes modeled and observed work
lines: work_mem default: 4 MB
hash_mem_multiplier default: 2.0
Sort and hash spills add work
Runtime sort method and batches are observations

narration.text: Sorting and hashing depend on estimated rows and width as well as memory limits. The defaults here are four megabytes of work memory and a hash memory multiplier of two. The cost model prices spilling when the estimated work exceeds its budget. A bounded sort for a small limit has different comparison work from a full sort.

Execution chooses its actual sort method and can grow hash batches when memory runs short. Q1’s reported top-N heap is a runtime result. They do not make the executor choose a different join tree when the estimates turn out wrong.

scenes.title: A small result can favor fast startup

screen.heading: A small result can favor fast startup
lines: For fraction f: startup + f × (total − startup)
All rows favor total cost
A cursor can favor earlier output
The page’s cursor example uses fraction 0.1

narration.text: When only a fraction of rows is wanted, the comparison can use startup plus that fraction of the remaining total cost. For all rows, total cost applies. A limit or fast-start cursor can therefore prefer an alternative with lower startup even when finishing every row would cost more.

The page’s cursor example uses a fraction of zero point one. Its merge join has a fractional cost near five hundred and eighty-nine, compared with about one thousand and seventy-two for the hash join. The requested amount of output changes the comparison.

scenes.title: The relation kind sets the scan menu

screen.heading: The relation kind sets the scan menu
lines: Plain tables: sequential, index, bitmap, TID
Kept subqueries: child planning, then a wrapper
Functions and VALUES have their own scan paths
Foreign tables ask their FDW

narration.text: Eligibility begins with what the relation represents. A plain table offers a sequential scan and, when their conditions hold, index, bitmap, and physical tuple identifier scans. A kept subquery is planned separately, then exposed through a SubqueryScan. A foreign table asks its foreign data wrapper for candidate paths.
Functions and VALUES have different sizing rules and basic scans. VALUES gives an exact row count. A function can use a support function’s row estimate or its declared row count.

scenes.title: Index eligibility comes before index cost

screen.heading: Index eligibility comes before index cost
lines: The index must be usable
A partial predicate must be proven
Key, operator family, and collation must match
Expression identity matters

narration.text: An index path first needs a usable index. An invalid index is skipped. For a partial index, the planner must prove that applicable conditions imply its predicate. Matching then checks the indexed key or expression, the operator family, and the collation. A condition’s other side cannot be volatile or depend on the same scanned relation.

Expression matching is not arbitrary algebra. The page shows that an expression such as identifier plus zero does not match the plain identifier key. A compatible cross-type operator can still match through its operator family.

scenes.title: Parameters and partial-index proof

screen.heading: Parameters and partial-index proof
lines: A custom plan can use actual parameter values
A generic parameter may not prove a value predicate
The page compares status = pending with $1
Independent predicate proof can still succeed

narration.text: A partial index can expose the difference between a custom plan and a generic plan. A custom plan has actual bound parameter values. A generic plan retains unknown parameters. An unknown status parameter cannot establish that every selected row has the particular pending status required by the page’s partial index.

This is about proof, not the presence of any parameter anywhere in the query. Conditions independent of the unknown value can still prove a predicate. Eligibility must be established before asking which index path has the lowest estimated cost.

scenes.title: Index-only eligibility and heap visits differ

screen.heading: Index-only eligibility and heap visits differ
lines: Needed columns must be returnable by the index
Planning uses the stored all-visible fraction
Execution checks live visibility
Writes can cause heap fetches; VACUUM can change them

narration.text: An index-only path requires all the needed underlying columns to be returnable by the index, and the index-only switch must permit the path. That eligibility does not promise zero heap visits. Planning prices heap fetches using the stored all-visible fraction, while execution checks the live visibility map.

The page’s write experiment reports three thousand and sixty heap fetches after changes, even though the stored visibility input has not caught up. After VACUUM, it reports zero. Keep the choice of an index-only plan separate from what visibility information lets that plan avoid during this execution.

scenes.title: Index types offer different paths

screen.heading: Index types offer different paths
lines: B-tree: ordinary ordering and parallel scans
GiST and SP-GiST: distance ordering
GIN and BRIN: bitmap scans
Bitmap combinations also undergo a cost comparison

narration.text: The access method constrains the menu. B-tree provides ordinary ordered scans and is the built-in index method that supports parallel index scans here. GiST and SP-GiST can provide distance ordering. GIN and BRIN supply bitmap scans. These capabilities are separate from a particular condition’s match.

Bitmap paths can combine usable index conditions with AND or OR. The planner does not simply combine every available index. It compares the estimated cost of combinations, including heap access. At execution, lossy bitmap pages require rechecks.

scenes.title: Search legal join orders

screen.heading: Search legal join orders
lines: One join relation per set of tables
Dynamic programming builds larger sets
Collapse limits constrain join lists
GEQO threshold applies to one join list

narration.text: The join search builds larger relation sets from smaller ones. Dynamic programming considers useful pairs and creates one join relation for a set of tables, regardless of which input order produced it. Outer, semi, anti, full, and lateral dependencies constrain which combinations are legal. An illegal combination gets no candidate relation.

The collapse limits, both eight by default, shape the join lists. GEQO is enabled by default and is selected at twelve items in a single join list. That threshold is not a count of every table anywhere in the statement. Genetic search samples orders and does not guarantee the best possible one.

scenes.title: Choose among eligible join methods

screen.heading: Choose among eligible join methods
lines: Nested loop: repeated inner execution
Parameterized path: needs an outer value
Hash join: build, then probe
Merge join: compatible clauses and ordered inputs

narration.text: A nested loop executes its inner input for outer rows. A parameterized inner path needs a value from another relation, which makes an index lookup possible for each outer value. In this implementation, nested loops support inner, left, semi, and anti joins; they do not implement right or full joins.

A hash join requires a usable hash clause: it builds a hash table from its inner input, then probes it with the outer input. A merge join uses compatible merge clauses and ordered inputs, supplied by scans or sorts.

scenes.title: The page’s join-method comparison

screen.heading: The page’s join-method comparison
lines: items joined to pending orders
Default hash total: 2,349.02
Forced merge total: 4,777.52
Forced nested loop total: 5,021.12

narration.text: In Q2, the page compares joining items to pending orders. The default hash join’s total is two thousand three hundred and forty-nine point zero two. Turning off hash joins exposes a merge alternative at four thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven point five two. Turning off both hash and merge joins exposes a nested loop at five thousand and twenty-one point one two.
Those are estimated costs under the named probe settings. The hash choice wins the ordinary total-cost comparison in this fixture. They are not elapsed-time measurements.

scenes.title: Reduce repeated work when reuse is eligible

screen.heading: Reduce repeated work when reuse is eligible
lines: Materialize: save rows for rescans
Memoize: cache parameterized inner results
Hashable keys and safety conditions apply
The forced serial example: 5,505 hits; 495 misses

narration.text: Materialize saves rows from an input so later rescans can read them again cheaply. Memoize instead caches the complete results of parameterized inner scans by their parameter values. Its path needs conditions such as hashable cache keys, repeated outer execution, and absence of unsafe volatile behavior.

The page’s forced serial Memoize example executes six thousand outer lookups and reports five thousand five hundred and five cache hits, with four hundred and ninety-five misses and no evictions. The page did not measure that query at the default parallel setting. A chosen cache can replace repeated inner execution only when an entry is complete.

scenes.title: Some subqueries become joins

screen.heading: Some subqueries become joins
lines: Eligible IN / EXISTS: semi joins
Eligible NOT EXISTS: anti joins
Top-level position and safety conditions apply
NOT IN remains a SubPlan

narration.text: Eligible IN and EXISTS subqueries can become semi joins, and eligible NOT EXISTS subqueries can become anti joins. The transformation is limited by position and safety. It searches top-level WHERE or join conditions through AND, with restrictions on available outer relations, volatility, and the shape of the subquery.

PostgreSQL seventeen adds a supported correlated IN pull-up case under those relation restrictions. NOT IN follows a different path and remains a SubPlan, even when non-null columns make the page’s two examples return the same rows.

scenes.title: Remaining subqueries become executable expressions

screen.heading: Remaining subqueries become executable expressions
lines: SubPlan: executable subquery expression
Direct correlation supplies outer parameters
Eligible empty parParam: lazy InitPlan
Dependency changes can require reevaluation

narration.text: A subquery that stays inside an expression becomes a SubPlan. Direct correlation supplies parameter values from the immediately enclosing level, and the inner plan is rescanned when evaluated. An eligible subquery with no direct input parameters can become an InitPlan whose output is evaluated lazily when needed.

An InitPlan is not necessarily executed once forever. Indirectly correlated dependencies can change on rescan and make its output pending again. The page describes that recalculation from source, without a new measurement. Hashing a remaining eligible ANY subplan also requires hashable strict comparisons and an estimated result that fits the hash memory budget.

scenes.title: CTE inlining has conditions

screen.heading: CTE inlining has conditions
lines: Default: eligible singly referenced SELECT can inline
NOT MATERIALIZED still has safety restrictions
Recursive, locking, writing, volatile CTEs do not inline
MATERIALIZED keeps separate planning

narration.text: An eligible singly referenced SELECT CTE is normally inlined. NOT MATERIALIZED allows a multiply referenced CTE to request inlining, but does not override the safety tests. A recursive CTE, a locking or data-modifying CTE, or one using volatile functions is not inlined. Multiply referenced outer self-reference is another restriction.

MATERIALIZED keeps the CTE separately planned and scanned. A data-modifying CTE is different: it has its own modifying subplan and runs to completion even when its output is unread. The spelling of WITH alone does not tell you which behavior applies.

scenes.title: A planning fence can still supply information

screen.heading: A planning fence can still supply information
lines: Materialized CTE statistics and pathkeys pass upward
The outer query cannot change the CTE’s plan
Recursive worktable sizing uses a factor
Estimated iterations differ from actual recursion

narration.text: In PostgreSQL seventeen, a separately planned, non-recursive materialized CTE can pass column statistics and ordering information upward. The outer query can use that information when pricing its own paths. It still cannot change the already chosen CTE plan. A planning fence therefore need not mean that all statistics are hidden.

Recursive planning uses estimates: the worktable factor defaults to ten, and the recursive cost calculation assumes ten iterations separately. Those are model inputs. Neither estimate is a measurement of how many times the particular recursive query will actually loop.

scenes.title: Order matters above the joins

screen.heading: Order matters above the joins
lines: Useful orderings influence earlier path selection
Grouping → windows → DISTINCT → ORDER BY
Then LockRows, Limit, ModifyTable as needed
Presorted, incremental, or full sorting

narration.text: The planner knows useful orderings before the join search finishes. Ordering needed for grouping, windows, distinctness, or final output can preserve an otherwise dearer path. It then builds upper stages in their required sequence: grouping, windows, distinctness, and ordering, followed by row locking, limit, or modification when needed.

Projection can be folded into a capable node or receive a separate Result. For ordering, an existing full order can avoid sorting, a matching prefix can support incremental sort, or a full sort may be required. A small limit changes bounded-sort costing, but cannot be pushed through every operation indiscriminately.

scenes.title: Upper operations have their own eligibility

screen.heading: Upper operations have their own eligibility
lines: Hash grouping needs hashable keys
Ordered aggregates rule out hashed grouping
Partial aggregation needs combine support
UNION ALL appends; UNION removes duplicates

narration.text: Hash grouping needs hashable grouping keys and cannot implement ordered or distinct aggregates. Partial aggregation requires combine support, with serialization support for internal transition states and other restrictions. Sorted grouping can use existing order. PostgreSQL seventeen can reorder grouping keys to fit input order when the feature’s conditions hold.

UNION ALL appends branches; UNION requires duplicate removal using eligible hashed or sorted alternatives. One costing limitation remains: the page says that per-group sorts inside an ordered aggregate are not priced, so those alternatives’ displayed costs are not directly comparable.

scenes.title: Prune before building child plans

screen.heading: Prune before building child plans
lines: Expand after restrictions are known
Immutable key constants can prune at plan time
Each surviving child has its own paths
Legacy constraint exclusion is distinct

narration.text: Partitioned planning expands the parent after its restrictions are known. Immutable comparisons of partition keys with constants can remove partitions at plan time. The planner then opens and plans the surviving children. Each child has its own candidates, and Append or MergeAppend combines the chosen child paths.

Legacy inheritance follows a different boundary. Its children are opened before immutable CHECK constraints are used for constraint exclusion, and the parent can itself contain rows. Runtime partition pruning belongs to the declarative partition plan’s pruning information, not to legacy CHECK exclusion.

scenes.title: Some pruning waits for parameters

screen.heading: Some pruning waits for parameters
lines: Startup pruning can use external values
Execution pruning can use PARAM_EXEC
Changed parameters can trigger another pruning pass
Generic-plan locks precede startup pruning

narration.text: When values are unavailable during planning, the planner can store pruning steps for the executor. Startup pruning uses suitable stable or external parameter values; execution-time pruning can use internal executor parameters and repeat when they change. The page’s parameter example forces a generic plan and reports twelve subplans removed at startup.

Plain EXPLAIN EXECUTE can show startup pruning because it starts the executor without reading rows. A generic cached plan still locks its range-table relations before that pruning. Child ordering also matters: compatible partition bounds can permit an ordered Append; otherwise sorted child streams may require MergeAppend.

scenes.title: Build partial paths, then price collection

screen.heading: Build partial paths, then price collection
lines: Parallel safety and eligibility come first
Partial paths divide rows among processes
CPU is divided; disk cost is not
Gather adds setup and tuple transfer

narration.text: Parallel planning starts with safety and eligibility. The statement and relation must permit worker execution before partial paths are built. A partial path produces a subset of the result in each process, and Gather or Gather Merge collects it. A parallel-restricted condition on a base relation can keep that scan serial.

Worker counts depend on relation sizes, thresholds, overrides, and the cap. Costing divides CPU work by the worker count plus the modeled leader share, but does not divide disk cost. Gather adds setup and tuple transfer costs.

scenes.title: Planning permission differs from runtime availability

screen.heading: Planning permission differs from runtime availability
lines: Workers Planned and Workers Launched differ
Leader execution handles missing workers
JIT needs plan flags, live jit, and a provider
This page’s build did not demonstrate compilation

narration.text: The plan asks for workers, but execution launches only those available. With fewer workers, or none, the leader still runs the plan. The tutorial’s idle server launched the requested workers; a shortfall is described from source rather than measured in its fixture. Planned and launched counts answer different questions.

JIT compilation also crosses a boundary. Planning sets flags when JIT is enabled and a nonnegative threshold is strictly exceeded by the plan’s total cost. Runtime compilation additionally needs the live JIT switch and a loadable provider. This page’s build lacks LLVM, so it demonstrates flag selection, not compiled execution.

scenes.title: Plan the source rows, then modify

screen.heading: Plan the source rows, then modify
lines: Source scans and joins are planned normally
ModifyTable performs the write
Row identity supports modification and rechecks
Write effects are not priced in ModifyTable’s cost

narration.text: Writes first plan how to find source rows, then add ModifyTable. The page’s update joins western customers to pending orders and computes the new amount. Extra row identity columns identify targets and support concurrency rechecks. Row locking has its own LockRows node when requested.

ModifyTable carries its input cost rather than pricing all write effects. Its row estimate represents output only with RETURNING. Writes and row-locking queries stay serial here; CREATE TABLE AS has a separate parallel-eligible inner-query case.

scenes.title: MERGE and partition routing cross the boundary

screen.heading: MERGE and partition routing cross the boundary
lines: MERGE WHEN clauses determine the source join type
The executor chooses the per-row action
Partitioned INSERT routing occurs at execution
EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes a write

narration.text: MERGE builds a source join whose type depends on which matched and unmatched actions the WHEN clauses request. The executor then chooses the applicable action for each row. Partitioned INSERT also leaves the target partition choice to executor routing, rather than expanding children like a partitioned UPDATE.

At READ COMMITTED, a concurrently changed row can require qualification rechecks against its newer version. The page describes those concurrency paths from source. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes writes, so the tutorial wraps its write measurements in a transaction and rolls them back.

scenes.title: Turn the selected path into an executable tree

screen.heading: Turn the selected path into an executable tree
lines: create_plan builds Plan nodes
Finalize internal parameter dependencies
Fix references
Record dependencies in PlannedStmt

narration.text: The chosen path is converted into executable Plan nodes. The mapping is close to one for one, but a hash join needs a Hash node and a merge input may need a Sort. Parent requirements also shape which columns the child must return.

Final passes attach subplans, finalize internal parameter dependencies for rescans, and fix references to child outputs or the flattened range table. PlannedStmt records relation and other dependencies, alongside parallel and JIT information.

scenes.title: Custom and generic plans use different inputs

screen.heading: Custom and generic plans use different inputs
lines: Custom: actual bound parameter values
Generic: unknown parameter values
Auto with parameters: first five custom
Then compare generic cost with custom average

narration.text: PREPARE saves an analyzed and rewritten plan source before creating an executable plan on demand. A custom plan uses actual bound values; a generic plan uses unknown parameters and can be reused. With parameters in ordinary automatic mode, the first five plans are custom.

After that, the cache compares generic estimated cost with the custom average including a planning charge. Switching on the sixth use is not guaranteed. Force modes override this choice; statements without parameters normally use a generic plan. These comparisons use estimates, not timings collected from earlier executions.

scenes.title: A generic estimate can hide a common value

screen.heading: A generic estimate can hide a common value
lines: Customer 7 custom estimate: 458
Customer 500 custom estimate: 10
Generic estimate: 15
The page’s plans all use the same index

narration.text: In the page’s skewed customer example, a custom plan estimates four hundred and fifty-eight orders for customer seven, but only ten for customer five hundred. The generic estimate is fifteen. All three use the same index-only access method, so the distinction here lies in the estimate.
The cache can prefer the generic cost after accounting for the average custom costs and planning charge. That does not make the generic estimate suitable for every value.

scenes.title: Refresh statistics and cached plans separately

screen.heading: Refresh statistics and cached plans separately
lines: DDL can invalidate dependent plans
search_path changes require revalidation
pg_statistic updates alone do not invalidate
A changed pg_class row can trigger rebuilding

narration.text: Dependent cached plans can be invalidated by relation definition changes, including index changes. Name resolution and row-security state also participate in revalidation. A change to an ordinary planner cost setting affects new planning, but does not itself replace an already valid generic plan.

ANALYZE needs a precise qualification: rewriting column statistics alone does not invalidate that generic plan. If the entire pg_class row stays unchanged and no other invalidation occurs, it can keep its old estimates. Changed size fields or stale catalog flags can rewrite that row, send invalidation, and cause rebuilding on next use.

scenes.title: Embedded statements have different cache owners

screen.heading: Embedded statements have different cache owners
lines: Static PL/pgSQL statements use saved SPI plans
Dynamic EXECUTE plans on each use
A non-inlined SQL function cache belongs to FmgrInfo
Owner and transaction validity govern reuse

narration.text: Static PL/pgSQL statements use saved SPI plans and follow the plan cache’s choice rules within a session. Dynamic EXECUTE uses a one-shot plan each time. A non-inlined SQL-language function has a different cache, owned by its calling FmgrInfo.

That owner normally follows the calling query, but a longer-lived owner can retain the cache within valid transaction and subtransaction boundaries. The tutorial measures ordinary query-scoped callers. It describes longer-lived reuse from source, so a blanket statement that every SQL-function cache expires at each statement boundary would lose the qualification.

scenes.title: Extensions can change inputs, paths, or a stage

screen.heading: Extensions can change inputs, paths, or a stage
lines: planner_hook can wrap or replace planning
Path hooks can edit candidates
FDWs supply foreign paths and plans
Custom paths still compete when added normally

narration.text: The extension interfaces operate at several boundaries. A planner hook can wrap or replace planning. Other hooks can change relation information or path lists. A foreign data wrapper supplies sizing, paths, and the selected foreign plan; eligible joins or upper operations can be pushed to a remote server.

Paths added through the normal path APIs still undergo cost comparisons. A custom scan provider can add CustomPaths and build a CustomScan if one wins. The page describes custom scan interfaces from source because the pinned core tree has no provider.

scenes.title: Capabilities and support functions feed the model

screen.heading: Capabilities and support functions feed the model
lines: Index AM flags constrain scan capabilities
amcostestimate prices an index path
Support functions may answer specialized requests
A NULL support answer leaves the fallback

narration.text: Index access-method flags tell the planner which scans, ordering, and returned columns are possible, while the cost callback supplies index estimates. Table access methods contribute relation size estimates. These inputs connect extension behavior to the same eligibility and costing stages.

A planner support function attached to a SQL function can answer specialized requests such as simplification, selectivity, cost, rows, or an index condition. A null answer means the planner falls back to the corresponding ordinary behavior. The page’s LIKE example derives an index range while retaining the needed filter.

scenes.title: Start diagnosis at the first divergence

screen.heading: Start diagnosis at the first divergence
lines: Compare estimates with actual rows per execution
Read from the leaves upward
Use actual rows × loops for total work
The page’s first error: customers 10 vs 98

narration.text: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan and its estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and adds observations. Compare a node’s estimated rows with its actual rows per execution, starting at the leaves. In the correlated customer example, the first divergence is the customer scan: ten estimated, ninety-eight observed.

The inner scan prints an average of ten actual rows across ninety-eight loops. Multiplying gives about nine hundred and eighty rows of total work; the join above reports the exact total, one thousand and eight. The difference comes from rounding the inner average.

scenes.title: A forced switch changes the comparison

screen.heading: A forced switch changes the comparison
lines: Penalty switches keep paths with a finite penalty
Gate switches prevent generation where applicable
Merge and hash full joins have an exception
A penalized winner does not prove alternatives absent

narration.text: Method switches have different behavior. Turning off a penalty switch, such as sequential scanning or nested loops, keeps paths but adds a finite penalty of ten billion. A generation gate, such as hash joins or merge joins for ordinary inner joins, prevents those paths from being built. Full joins have an exception.

The page demonstrates a penalized sequential winner even with an eligible bitmap alternative that is penalized too. A large printed cost therefore does not prove the absence of alternatives. Check eligibility and complete ordinary costs before interpreting the original choice.

scenes.title: Match the observation to the question

screen.heading: Match the observation to the question
lines: SETTINGS: non-default flagged planner settings
MEMORY: measured planner allocations
EXPLAIN EXECUTE: current cached-plan choice
GENERIC_PLAN cannot be combined with ANALYZE

narration.text: EXPLAIN SETTINGS lists non-default settings flagged for planner explanation; it does not list every session setting. MEMORY reports planner allocations, while SUMMARY can report planning time. The page quotes memory figures from one platform and records no timings, so memory comparisons are not elapsed-time measurements.

For saved statements, EXPLAIN EXECUTE shows the plan chosen now, and generic and custom counters show usage. GENERIC_PLAN permits inspection with unknown parameters but cannot be combined with ANALYZE.

scenes.title: Keep the page’s evidence limits visible

screen.heading: Keep the page’s evidence limits visible
lines: Measured fixtures are distinct from source-only behavior
No compiled JIT demonstration
Custom scan interfaces have no core provider here
Runtime counts do not train the planner

narration.text: The page separates experiments from source-only explanations. Its build cannot demonstrate compiled JIT, and no core custom scan provider exercises those interfaces. The memory figures describe this platform’s allocations. Forced settings expose behavior under named conditions rather than establishing recommended configuration.

The planner’s estimates come from stored statistics, live sizes, and settings. Executor row counts are printed and discarded; the page’s no-feedback conclusion rests on those inputs and instrumentation lifetime. Repeating the same execution does not by itself teach the planner the observed cardinalities.

scenes.title: Q1 connects the whole process

screen.heading: Q1 connects the whole process
lines: Stored density and frequencies → row estimates
Scan and join candidates → path comparison
Selected path → executable plan
Execution observes; changed inputs lead to new choices

narration.text: Q1 connects the process. Stored density and current page counts size orders and customers. Common-value frequencies estimate pending orders and western customers. Scan and join candidates compete; ordering and the five-row limit shape the upper work. The selected final path is constructed and finalized into an executable statement.

The run observes three thousand and nineteen orders, two hundred customers, and two hundred and ninety joined rows. It executes the chosen tree and adapts only within its allowed decisions. Statistics maintenance, schema changes, settings used in new planning, or the cache’s choice can change a later plan. The observations themselves are not planning feedback.
